A comparison was made between the use of antibiotics such as ampicillin, ampicillin/clavulanic acid, or penicillin versus no treatment following an initial course of intravenous antibiotics. This analysis included data from one trial involving 63 women and six trials involving 740 women. The trials evaluated the effectiveness of antibiotic regimens with poor activity against penicillin-resistant anaerobic bacteria compared to regimens with good activity. Notably, six out of seven trials tested the combination of clindamycin and gentamicin. 2. A small trial involving 16 women reported treatment failure when comparing oral ofloxacin/clindamycin to intravenous clindamycin/gentamicin for postpartum endometritis. 3. The quality of evidence supporting these recommendations was graded as low to very low overall. This indicates a need for further research to strengthen the evidence base. 4. The combination of clindamycin and an aminoglycoside, particularly gentamicin, appears to be more effective than cephalosporins or penicillins in treating postpartum endometritis. However, more data on side effects are needed to fully understand the balance between benefits and potential harms. Clindamycin and gentamicin are generally not associated with serious adverse effects in clinical practice. 5. There is no cost-related data to determine the comparative cost-effectiveness of various antibiotic regimens. However, clindamycin is consistently associated with higher costs and less favorable cost-effectiveness in many settings. 6. Healthcare providers and policymakers in high-income settings are likely to value the added benefits of clindamycin and gentamicin over other antibiotic classes due to better treatment outcomes and manageable side effects. In contrast, providers in low-income settings may place less value on these benefits due to cost and accessibility issues. 7. The panel acknowledged that preferences for antibiotic regimens might vary based on local policies, clinicians’ experience, knowledge of antimicrobial resistance patterns, maternal allergies, and the availability and cost of antibiotics. 8. It is technically feasible to include clindamycin and gentamicin in existing protocols for postpartum endometritis in healthcare facilities. However, while gentamicin is inexpensive and widely available, clindamycin is more expensive and not readily accessible in all settings, particularly in low-resource areas. 9. The use of clindamycin is likely to increase healthcare costs, especially in low-resource settings. 10. Despite the burden of maternal peripartum infections, the evidence supporting the recommendations in this guideline is generally rated as low or very low. According to the GRADE methodology, further research is likely to impact the direction and strength of these recommendations. 11. Critical gaps in current evidence regarding the prevention and treatment of infectious conditions around childbirth were identified. These gaps were prioritized based on their potential to improve maternal and neonatal outcomes, feasibility, and ability to address health inequities. 12. Evidence is lacking for widely used practices such as prophylactic antibiotics to prevent infections in women with episiotomy or those undergoing normal low-risk labor. 13. Research gaps include the comparative effectiveness and safety of chlorhexidine versus povidone-iodine for vaginal cleansing during cesarean sections, the timing of vaginal cleansing relative to cesarean sections, and women’s preferences regarding perineal/pubic shaving before vaginal birth. 14. Additional gaps include the effects of routine prophylactic antibiotics on perineal wound infection morbidity in women with episiotomy, the impact of prolonged rupture of membranes on maternal and neonatal infections, and the effects of administering antibiotics before cesarean sections on neonatal antibiotic resistance and long-term infant health. 15. The guideline aims to improve maternal and neonatal health outcomes and the quality of care. Dissemination and implementation of the recommendations should involve clinicians, policymakers, and other stakeholders at international, national, and local levels. 16. The recommendations will be disseminated through WHO regional and country offices, ministries of health, professional organizations, and other relevant entities. The guideline will also be available on the WHO website and in the WHO Reproductive Health Library. 17. To increase awareness, a short commentary will be published in a peer-reviewed journal, and the guideline will be presented at scientific conferences. The executive summary will be translated into six UN languages. 18. Technical assistance will be provided to WHO regional offices for translating the full guideline into UN languages. The GREAT Network will support lowand middle-income countries in adapting and implementing the guideline. 19. The guideline will be updated five years after publication unless significant new evidence necessitates earlier revision. The Steering Group will monitor research developments and address any concerns about the validity of recommendations. 20. Monitoring and evaluation of guideline implementation should occur at health-service, regional, and country levels using clearly defined criteria and indicators. Data collection will assess the impact on national policies and adherence to recommendations. 21. Indicators to monitor include the proportion of women undergoing cesarean sections who receive antibiotic prophylaxis, the proportion of women with preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM) who receive antibiotic prophylaxis, and the incidence of surgical wound infections after cesarean sections. 22. The guideline will undergo systematic review and updating processes to ensure it remains current and evidence-based. WHO welcomes suggestions for additional questions to include in future updates.
